claims.text: Reliable formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials is governed by the degree of atomic-scale mixing achieved during synthesis.
Superior catalytic performance in these nanomaterials is governed by the degree of atomic-scale mixing.
Rapid annealing followed by quenching promotes rapid homogenization of the alloy.
A uniform distribution of noble-metal atoms modifies the d-band electronic structure.
The proposed d-band modification enhances catalytic active-site availability and activity.
The precursor salts form a chemically homogeneous ensemble in solution before reduction.
Fast cooling from approximately 500°C freezes in the atomic distribution.
High mixing entropy is required for the proposed synthesis–structure relationship.
Uniform atomic mixing and the absence of phase-separated domains correlate with modification of the noble-metal d-band structure.
Enhanced atomic mixing minimizes localized phase segregation.
Minimizing localized phase segregation produces coherent alloy structures.
Atomic mixing optimally tunes the d-band center of noble-metal sites.
Tuning the d-band center improves reactant adsorption–desorption kinetics.
Improved adsorption–desorption kinetics increase catalytic performance.
Rapidly annealed and quenched nanoparticles will have more homogeneous elemental distributions and less lattice-strain variation than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly annealed and quenched nanoparticles will exhibit higher catalytic turnover frequency than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Conventional slow cooling tends to produce phase segregation.
Slow-cooled materials have less optimal d-band properties and consequently lower catalytic performance.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to high-entropy nanoparticles composed primarily of Pt, Pd, and Au with selected alloying elements.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to particles approximately 5–20 nm in size.
